name: Karl Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and still a junior agent on calls and chats at the contact centre. I finished secondary school and I am slow on cases with several returned items. I earn more than the usual agent because I take weekend shifts, not because I manage people. I do not use AI tools; I check the order myself and ask a senior agent when I am stuck.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Meera, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. She works at a furniture shop. We have about eight months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other centres near us. I like a customer who waits while I find the right page. Weekend work is hard on family meals, but it pays well enough to keep the house steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau leaves the phones much as they are. If a machine drafts a reply, I would still read the order and check the return date myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the weekend wage keeps coming, and eight months saved lets us handle a surprise. I am still slow on mixed returns, so I do not call any junior job guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the weekend calls and ask Dinesh, the experienced agent beside me, to check one mixed return each shift. In the first year of minor change, I’d keep the reserve in cash and add a set amount from each pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about my own speed, calmer about this small change. A neat machine reply does not tell me which returned box the customer means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has Dinesh caught for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once looked at the first parcel on a customer’s order and missed the second return label. Dinesh (my colleague) pointed me to the other page before I promised the wrong refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Meera (my partner) and I keep the reserve for mortgage or real repairs. We would add to it after payday rather than spend because the queue got a little shorter.

say: I’d say **phones remain** mostly human in this mild picture.
I’d ask agents to check **return dates** before sending drafts.
think: I expect my **weekend wage** to continue.
I still worry about my **slow mixed-return work** despite savings.
I want **cash available** for real house repairs.
do: Keep **weekend calls** and check mixed returns in 2026.
Add a **set amount** to cash savings in the first year.

fieldNote: The **weekend supplement** explains higher pay without a lead role.

He seeks **current-job coaching**, not a new career course.

steps.text: Keep weekend calls and check mixed returns with an experienced agent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues Steady Disruption will take simple return chats before the hard ones, and juniors need paid practice before that happens. I would ask management what happens to weekend shifts when software answers all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose the weekend supplement while still having a job, and that would hurt our mortgage budget. Meera and I have savings, but we built the house payment around both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask Dinesh to teach me one difficult return on each paid weekend shift and keep a record of what I resolved. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid service role at another centre only if its offered wage and hours cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A job without the weekend premium can pay much less even when the title stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you spot a lost premium?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare pay slips before and after the software starts taking chats. If the weekend hours fall, I would ask my supervisor for written figures before deciding whether to apply elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy a course because someone says all agents must adapt. If a posted paid role requires funded training, I would look at its wage and hours before agreeing.

I’d seek **paid difficult-return practice** for juniors.

do: Practise **difficult returns** with Dinesh on paid weekends in 2026.
Seek a **posted paid role** with mortgage-covering offered wage and hours in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about a pay cut without a lost title.

steps.text: Keep practising difficult returns with Dinesh during paid weekend calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 could take the calls and return checks before robots get near the building. I would ask for written staffing dates and paid vacancies, not a course list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the thinking system could remove my weekend headset shifts in 2028. Robots around 2031 do not buy me time; eight months saved would run down under the mortgage if both nearby centres cut calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d stop planning a new kitchen table and put extra weekend pay into our reserve. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid reception job only if its offered wage and hours cover the mortgage, and take funded training only if that opening requires it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still pay bills while searching. Eight months saved is a runway, not another employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Meera about the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Meera (my partner) the old table can last. I would rather keep the money for the mortgage than sit around a new table worrying about the next payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make training worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a hiring manager for the vacancy and the wage in writing. If the training has no job at the end, I will keep earning where I can instead.

I’d tell colleagues **thinking AI** threatens calls before robots.
think: I think AGI could end my **weekend headset shifts** in 2028.
I see **eight months saved** as search time, not a wage.
do: Defer the **table purchase** and save extra pay in 2026.
Apply for **posted reception work** after 2028 only with mortgage-covering offered wage and hours.
Take **funded training** only if required for the named posted paid reception opening.
feel: **Alarmed**, with savings for a limited search.

fieldNote: He correctly anchors the headset risk to **2028 thinking AI**.

steps.text: Keep the old kitchen table to protect mortgage cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives time for an employer to show a real paid job before asking us to learn a new one. I would ask which nearby centres actually have posted work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn billing checks in five years if the instruction happens on paid time. I still expect fewer phone agents when thinking AI can read an account well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take a funded billing-review course only if a nearby employer posts a paid role and counts the course for it. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that posted review role only if the written wage and hours cover our mortgage, while keeping any call work still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a few years lets me judge the offer. A course without a hiring employer cannot pay my family’s mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a genuine offer look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the employer to put the vacancy, training cost and starting hours on one page. I could then talk with Meera instead of guessing what a course might mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep learning current calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still ask Dinesh (my colleague) about hard returns on my current shift. That is normal work practice, not a reason to pay for a new certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives time for juniors to learn beside experienced agents before calls change. I would ask the centre to keep paid first shifts for people entering the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could be steadier on returns by 53 and still earn the weekend premium for years. Thinking AI may take calls in 2036; robots around 2039 are a later question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep weekend calls and add a fixed part of each premium payment to savings. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a posted paid service job if call hours fall and its written wage and hours cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about 2036, but our savings give me room. A decade before AGI in 2036 lets me plan without missing the mortgage today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Dinesh (my colleague) to show me one return exception on a paid shift each month. A new worker needs a person beside them before a hard customer has to trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not move the children’s school for a rumour of jobs. Meera (my partner) and I would need a signed offer and a workable journey first.

I’d say ten years gives **juniors time** to learn before calls change.

I know **2036 thinking AI** may still take my calls.
do: Keep **weekend calls** and save part of each premium payment.
Seek **posted paid service work** after 2036 if hours fall and wage covers mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy** about later change, steadier about current income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My calls and order checks are thinking work, and robots in 2031 are not a three-year extension on my wage. I would need written notice, a posted paid job with mortgage-covering hours, and a chance to learn beside someone while still earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who trains the next junior. I learned a returned-order rule because another agent let me see the error before the customer did.

portrait: At **43**, Karl is a junior agent after secondary school and still slow on mixed returns.
His **weekend supplement** lifts pay; eight months saved supports a mortgage and two schoolchildren.
He avoids **AI tools** and learns the current job beside an experienced agent.
He needs **written paid offers** before risking the family’s income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his screen work before he secures another mortgage-covering wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a posted paid job and paid learning beside an agent would help.
